title: Epiphany: chalking the door
hook: in some countries families chalk the year and the magi's initials over their door

segments.voice: Yesterday, the New Year and the Holy Name, given on the eighth day. Your line was his name was jesus. What name or word did you begin the year with? Day one thousand fifteen.

Above a front door in a quiet street, in white chalk, there's a short line of numbers, letters and little crosses. The numbers are the new year, split in two at either end. In the middle are three capital letters: C, M, B. It looks like a code, and in a way it is. In parts of Europe and in Catholic and some Lutheran homes elsewhere, families stand at the door in early January with a stick of chalk, sometimes blessed by a priest, and write it there together. Then it stays, fading slowly, until next year. Today, Epiphany.

Epiphany is the church's word for a showing, an appearing. In Western churches the feast remembers the wise men, the magi, coming to see the child, and through them, the child being shown to the whole world. Matthew tells it: "there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem." Look closely at what Matthew says and doesn't. He doesn't say how many came. He doesn't call them kings. He doesn't give their names. Tradition counted three, perhaps because of the three gifts, and later named them Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar. That's where the C, the M and the B come from. But there's a second reading of the letters, in Latin: Christus mansionem benedicat. May Christ bless this house. And here's the detail that makes the chalk make sense. Matthew says where the wise men found the child: "And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh." Into the house. Not the manger. In Matthew's telling, the family is in an ordinary home, and strangers from far away are coming through its door. So the chalk marks a front door as a place where Christ has been welcomed, and where guests, and the year itself, will come in. This week has run from the O Antiphons through Christmas Eve, the Nativity, Stephen, the Innocents and the Holy Name. In some Western churches, Epiphany closes the Christmas season, and it ends at a doorway.

Here's the practice: bless your front door. If you can, go and stand at it, or picture it clearly. Touch the frame. Think of everyone who comes through it: the people you live with, guests, deliveries, the neighbor who knocks. Think of the year that's about to walk in. If you have chalk and want to, you can write the year and the three letters above it. If you pray, you can say the old Latin line's meaning: may Christ bless this house. If you don't, simply stand there and wish this doorway well. The bell holds the time.
Epiphany. A showing: the feast of the wise men finding the child in the house, kept in some homes by chalking the year and C, M, B over the door.
Your line: bless this house. Today, each time you walk through your front door, slow down for one step and remember who the house is open to. Day one thousand fifteen.

howItsDone: In Catholic and some Lutheran and Anglican households, families chalk the year and the letters C, M, B over the door around Epiphany, sometimes with chalk blessed at church; in some places a priest visits to bless homes.

notes: Claims rule: 'Epiphany means a showing, an appearing' is a gloss on the feast name (Greek epiphaneia); confirm. 'People counted three because of the three gifts' is a common explanation, stated softly; the three gifts are in Matthew 2:11.
The names Caspar, Melchior, Balthasar are given as later tradition; no date given.
'In some Western churches, Epiphany closes the Christmas season': calendars differ (Baptism of the Lord, Candlemas); confirm or soften.
Day 1015 is a week end; the teach glances back at days 1009–1014. Orthodox Theophany is left for tomorrow.
Original: μάγοι is the plural in Matthew 2:1; confirm pronunciation.

Editor: the reason for 'three' is now tradition's and hedged ('perhaps'); 'not the stable' changed to 'not the manger' (no Gospel names a stable); 'Epiphany means' rephrased as the church's word, matching day 1003's handling of Advent.
